column1: # Algerian Darija markers written in Arabic script.
# weight:  strong = distinctly Darija, one occurrence is enough to call it
#          weak   = used in Darija but also in MSA or other dialects, needs corroboration
# NEEDS NATIVE-SPEAKER REVIEW. Nothing here has been checked by a native Algerian speaker.
# Blocker B7 in the plan. The list is machine-assembled to get detection working and to give a
# reviewer something to correct rather than a blank file — correcting a wrong weight is far less
# How to review it: the sections below are ordered roughly by confidence. Copula, pronouns and
# question words are the safest; the French-borrowing and food sections are the most Algerian and
# also the easiest to get subtly wrong. Anything you disagree with is more likely to be wrong than
# Two specific risks a reviewer should look for:
#   - Moroccan/Tunisian terms wrongly included as Algerian
#   - terms marked strong that are actually common in MSA news copy
# Terms are normalised on load, so writing them with or without harakat makes no difference.
# --- copula / pronouns: the strongest single signal ------------------------------------
# MACHINE-GENERATED EXPANSION — everything below this line is unreviewed.
# Assembled without a native speaker, deliberately conservative: where a term is shared with
# Moroccan or Tunisian Darija it is marked `weak` even when it is common in Algeria, because a
# false `strong` actively misclassifies text while a false `weak` only fails to help.
# --- verbs: the most productive class, and mostly Maghrebi-wide -------------------------------
# --- negation: the circumfix is one of the clearest Maghrebi signals --------------------------
# --- French borrowings: among the most distinctly Algerian markers ------------------------------
# Lookup is exact per token, so an inflected or article-prefixed form needs its own row. This is
# why "وصفة المحاجب بالخضرة" was read as MSA: محاجب is listed, المحاجب was not.
